lesson.title: Watching a Signal Unfold: The Time-Domain View
lesson.summary: The time domain is the ordinary way of looking at a signal, its value plotted against time, which is exactly what an oscilloscope screen shows.
lesson.body:
A signal, by definition, is a quantity such as voltage or current that changes over time, so the most direct way to look at one is to plot its value against time and watch it unfold. That plot, v(t) or i(t) against t, is the time domain, and it is the native language of an oscilloscope. Everything about the physical shape of a waveform, its rise time, its peak value, whether it overshoots or rings after a transition, exactly when a switch closes, is visible directly on a time domain trace in a way that is not obvious from any other representation.

The Period prerequisite is what lets you read a time domain plot quantitatively rather than just qualitatively. The period T is the horizontal distance between two corresponding points on the waveform, say between one rising edge and the next rising edge that looks identical. Once you can identify T on the screen, you immediately know the fundamental frequency f0 = 1/T, which is the anchor for every harmonic frequency discussed in earlier chapters.

Here is a fully worked example of reading a time domain plot quantitatively. Consider ordinary North American household power, a sine wave with frequency 60 Hz and a peak value of about 170 V (this comes from the standard 120 V rms rating, since peak = rms times the square root of 2, and 120 times 1.414 is about 170). Write it as v(t) = 170 sin(2 pi times 60 times t). Its period is T = 1/60 = 16.67 milliseconds, which is the spacing you would measure between successive peaks on a scope trace. Now find the instantaneous value at t = 2 milliseconds. The angle is omega t = 2 pi (60)(0.002) = 0.754 radians, which is 43.2 degrees. The sine of 43.2 degrees is about 0.685, so v(0.002 s) = 170 times 0.685 = about 116.4 V. That is exactly the kind of question the time domain view answers directly: what is the signal doing at this particular instant.

The time domain has a real limitation, though. For a complicated, non-sinusoidal waveform, the trace shows you the overall shape, but it does not directly tell you which harmonics are combining to produce that shape, or how large each one is. Answering that requires replotting the same signal sorted by frequency instead of by time, which is exactly the frequency domain view covered next.
